mappings.note: POEM item: how the King's attitude transformed. The before and after are both on the page. Retrieval in extended writing, not the CG-ENG2 branch.

Craft activity (complete a paper web) whose only language demand is decorating it with words and phrases learnt from the poem. No LO covers making an object; the reading goal is cited because the words are harvested from the text. C-ENG2.2-LO-2 was rejected -- no dictionary or thesaurus is involved.
POEM MCQ naming the main character (King Bruce of Scotland). Retrieval. (Attached concept 'The River as a character' is misassigned -- this is the spider poem.)
POEM MCQ on his opening feeling ('sad and lonely'). Stated detail.
POEM MCQ on what he was trying to do (a great deed for his people). Stated detail.
POEM MCQ on why he was sad -- the stanza gives the reason. Retrieval. (Attached concept 'Why River is capitalised' is misassigned.)
POEM MCQ on what he considered doing in despair ('give it all up'). Quoted detail.
POEM MCQ on what appeared (a spider). Stated detail.
POEM MCQ on what the spider hung from ('a silken, filmy clue'). Quoted phrase, retrieval.
POEM MCQ on the spider's destination. Stated detail. (Answer carries the Amazon advert leak.)
POEM MCQ on the number of attempts (nine). Stated number.
POEM MCQ on what followed each attempt (fell, dizzy). Stated detail.
POEM MCQ on the King's opinion of the spider ('foolish thing'). Quoted judgement, retrieval.
POEM MCQ, did the spider stop trying. Yes/no on a stated fact.
POEM MCQ on how it finally succeeded (climbed slowly, steadily). Stated detail.
POEM MCQ on what the King shouted ('Bravo, bravo!'). Quoted.
POEM MCQ on the lesson the King learnt -- the moral, a whole-poem reading. CG-ENG2 branch, which is why it differs from the neighbouring recall MCQs.
POEM MCQ, what the spider symbolises. Symbolism is never stated; CG-ENG2 branch, not retrieval.
POEM MCQ on how the poem ends. Plot fact, retrieval -- unlike the symbol item above.
POEM MCQ on where the spider was climbing (the ceiling dome). Quoted detail.
POEM MCQ asking what feeling the repeated attempts show -- a trait inferred from behaviour, not a stated word. CG-ENG2 branch.
POEM MCQ on why the King watched: the stanza says 'To see what the spider would do'. Retrieval, so not the inference branch. (NODIA watermark in the answer.)
Assertion-Reason on the King's despair; requires judging whether R explains A. Reasoning, CG-ENG2 branch.
Assertion-Reason separating the difficulty of the thread from the cause of the dizziness. Causal reasoning, CG-ENG2 branch.
Assertion-Reason where R inverts the poem's logic (the spider inspired rather than discouraged). Testing a claim, CG-ENG2 branch.
Assertion-Reason: both true but R explains a later stage than A. Fine-grained causal reasoning, CG-ENG2 branch.
POEM item: the King's mood at the start ('lonely mood to think'). One-line retrieval.
POEM item: what he was attempting for his people. Stated. Retrieval.
POEM item: what he considered doing in despair. Quoted line. Retrieval.
POEM item: what dropped at that moment. Stated. Retrieval.
POEM item: number of attempts ('nine brave attempts'). Retrieval.
POEM item: the King's reaction after counting. Quoted. Retrieval.
POEM item: how far the spider was from its door ('only a foot'). Stated measure. Retrieval.

Reflective writing task: the stem is only its sentence-starters ('This experience taught me that...'), and the expected answer is a personal narrative. C-ENG4.2-LO-1 (narratives) over C-ENG4.1-LO-1, because the demand is a recounted experience, not sentence ordering. Stem is truncated -- the instruction line is missing.
POEM item: how the King felt at the start and why. Both quoted. Retrieval. (Attached concept 'Why River is capitalised' is misassigned.)
POEM item: what the spider does after its first fall. Narrated in the stanza. Retrieval.
POEM item: the big lesson the King learnt. A moral drawn from the whole poem, so CG-ENG2 branch rather than the plot-fact LO.
POEM item: how the spider's persistence changed the King's actions -- the poem narrates the change ('braced his mind... tried once more'). Retrieval, not thematic inference.
POEM item: describe the spider's efforts and obstacles. Assembled from stated detail. Retrieval.
POEM item: explain the moral with reference to the King's experience. Theme plus textual support, CG-ENG2 branch.
POEM item: how the poet builds suspense. Narrative technique, never stated. CG-ENG2 branch.
POEM item: the spider as a symbol of resilience. Symbolic reading, CG-ENG2 branch.
Hypothetical: advise the King before the spider appears. Entirely outside the poem, which is the goal's 'go beyond the text' clause; no LO covers inventing an intervention.
Two-part: recount a personal challenge (a narrative, C-ENG4.2-LO-1) and then apply the poem to it (beyond the text, CG-ENG2). Both cited because neither half is incidental.

Write a thought bubble in the spider's voice. Composition in an assumed persona, so the creative-writing LO; C-ENG4.2-LO-2 was rejected -- it is an interior monologue, not a dialogue drawn from the story.
POEM extract (opening stanza) with four sub-questions, all answerable from the lines. Retrieval.
POEM extract ('tried and tried') with four literal sub-questions. Retrieval.

Stem is corrupted: it is the filled-in see/hear/smell/taste/touch table of the preceding sensory-memory activity, with the real question ('How does this memory make you feel?') tacked on the end. That question is about the student's own experience, which only the goal statement covers.
POEM extract ('Up, up it ran') with four literal sub-questions. Retrieval.
POEM extract ('delicate thread') with four literal sub-questions. Retrieval.
POEM extract ('Bravo, bravo!') with four sub-questions answerable from the stanza. Retrieval.
POEM extract (final stanza) with four literal sub-questions. Retrieval. (Flipkart advert leak in the answer.)
POEM extract (the spider drops) with four literal sub-questions. Retrieval.
POEM extract ('a long way up to the ceiling dome') with four literal sub-questions. Retrieval.

Extract from the Helen Keller piece ('Three Days to See'), a third text inside this chapter. Sub-question (i) is a collocation/word-choice item (C-ENG2.2-LO-2) while (ii) and (iii) ask why the earth is called 'sleeping' and for a reason -- figurative interpretation (C-ENG2.1-LO-2). Both cited.
'Three Days to See': explain how touch compensates for sight and hearing, with reference to the text. Requires synthesising an argument the text implies. CG-ENG2 branch.
'Three Days to See': why the author believes sight is most wonderful. Her reasons are stated, so retrieval rather than inference -- contrast the 'how might this guide us' item, which got CG-ENG2.
Asks how the author's view should change our behaviour towards people with disabilities -- an application far outside the text. Goal level, no LO fits.
'According to the author', the significance of imagining sensory loss -- flagged as answerable from the text. Retrieval.
How the author encourages readers to approach everyday sensory experience -- the essay's central message, drawn from the whole text rather than one line. CG-ENG2 branch.
